query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a modest amount of titanium (~5 at.%) into the equiatomic CoCrFeNi alloy will promote an in‐situ formation of a continuous, self-healing Ti‐rich oxide scale under sliding that maintains reduced friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a primarily FCC structure that exhibits increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to conventional oxidation and microstructural degradation.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding approximately 5 at.% Ti into the CoCrFeNi matrix.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in air at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C under a controlled load and sliding speed.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a fine, continuous Ti-rich oxide scale at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures the modified alloy maintains a refined microstructure similar to the base alloy, while at elevated temperatures the reactive Ti oxidizes to form a lubricious and protective oxide film. This oxide film acts as a diffusion barrier that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby reducing the coefficient of friction and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-modified CoCrFeNi alloy is predicted to exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance of the starting CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which shows acceptable wear and friction at room temperature but degrades due to increased oxidation and microstructural instability at higher temperatures.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under similar sliding loads and atmospheric conditions over the tested temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C). Long-term cyclic sliding behavior and potential effects on other mechanical properties are not addressed here and require further study.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti content for achieving a stable oxide film without adversely affecting the alloy’s bulk mechanical properties remains to be precisely determined, and the long-term durability of the Ti-induced oxide film under repeated sliding cycles needs further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the base CoCrFeNi alloy and one modified with ~5 at.% Ti. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled load and speed at incremental temperatures from room temperature up to 800 °C in air. Characterize the wear tracks using SEM, EDS, and XRD to assess the formation, continuity, and composition of the oxide scale.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate quantified by mass loss or wear track depth
Oxide scale composition and morphology (via SEM, EDS, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not display a statistically significant decrease in the coefficient of friction and wear rate (relative to the base alloy) across the temperature range, or if the anticipated continuous Ti-rich oxide layer is not detected on the wear surface at higher temperatures, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
